The Fundamental movement started in the early 20th century as a reaction to the liberalizing of Christianity. At the time of the movement, the KJV was the major translation in use in American Christianity. Over time, large segments of the movement (hereafter derogatorily called "fundies") stagnated &, instead of holding rigorously to the fundamental doctrines of Christianity, began to hold rigorously to the culture surrounding the Fundamental movement. A part of said culture was/is the use of the KJV.

Today, the religious descendants of those fundies have built a doctrine around using the KJV and only the KJV, asserting that all modern translations are corrupt because the translators are only seeking sales, or they are attempts to subvert Christianity with false Bibles that remove or alter significant passages. There are varying degrees to this obsession with the KJV with some holding that you can only be saved out of a KJV Bible while others merely prefer the KJV because that's what they are familiar with.

It is primarily due to the fundies (who are often very vocal in their preference for the KJV) that there is a significant KJV movement. All the English bibles say the same thing

No they really don't. Some versions translate on a word for word basis and others on a contextual bases. In bible study one thing that amazed us was how one passage could be written in so many different ways depending on the version on the Bible you had. Sometimes the words chosen were so different it seemed to change the meaning. So, knowing what version you have and the technique in how it was translated is important.

I didn't say what you think I said. I said, "Pretty much," which is accurate. You definitely know that you're reading the Bible whenever you read it, whether a "liberal" translation, such as the NRSV or NIV, or a "conservative" translation, like the NKJV or NASB. the exceptions are some paraphrases (The Message), and one or two "versions" that were specifically "translated" to fulfill a particular goal. The differences between a word for word version and a less word for word version or paraphrase are far fewer than you might expect. I've read the Greek New Testament many times through (and portions of the Hebrew Old Testament), and there is a good deal of room for a translation to make decisions between synonyms. This in no way diminishes the inspiration of Scripture, by the way, because the words "Inspired of God" refer to the autographa, the original documents themselves. I agree that there are mistakes made in modern translations, but there were mistakes made in the KJV as well. They are insignificant. The REAL problem comes with the use of specific manuscripts. This is not the place for a commentary on textual criticism, but that's the core issue that we face as students of the Scriptures. For example, John 7:53-8:11 was not included in the two manuscripts that form the basis of the Westcott and Hort Greek New Testament. Why? Well, because that passage is deleted from the manuscripts on which that Greek New Testament is built. That's why you'll find the comment in the NIV that "the oldest manuscripts do not contain..." or similar words. I believe the NIV translators were wrong about this, because MANY manuscripts contain this section, even though those two don't. There is a bit more to the study of translation and translations than a simple, "word for word" or "paraphrased" approach.
I hope you'll consider what I've written.
